name: Ivan Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a thirty-person firm in a commuter town, and my clients are small businesses: cafés, gyms, hair salons and people selling things online. I prepare their year-end accounts and tax returns, and I use AI tools every day, to match payments to invoices, draft the notes and summarise what's changed since last year. I like the owners, they're grafters, the woman who runs the gym on Mill Lane opens at five every morning. What wears me out is that I'm quick but I still make rookie errors, and Mr Brennan, my manager, has started saying speed isn't the same as judgment.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the error he points to most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Treating everything an online seller buys as stock, when some of it's equipment. The AI sorts it fast and I trust it too much. I'm learning, but slower than I'd like. Paula, my girlfriend, is a physiotherapist, and she says I'd make a terrible patient because I'd skip the exercises once I felt better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a good tool, and people who use it well still get ahead. At work I'd keep showing Mr Brennan how much time I save. Online I'd probably post a few tips for small business owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I'm quick with the tools, I've got about five months saved, and there are other firms nearby if I wanted to move. It gives me time to learn the judgment side, which I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, pass my exams, and ask Mr Brennan to put me on the trickier online-seller files. I'd save a bit more, two hundred a month, towards a house deposit with Paula. And I'd start sketching a plan for my own small practice in a few years, because that's always been the goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite optimistic, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your own practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my grandad had a fruit stall and my dad had a corner shop, and both of them worked for themselves. I want to be the one who builds something, not the one waiting for a rise. In my family, you don't really count as grown up until you've got your own name over a door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you, even in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe that I get complacent, like Paula says. If the tools make me fast, I might never get properly good.

say: I'd say people who use AI **well still get ahead**.
I'd post **tips** for small business owners online.
think: It's **good for me**: quick with tools and five months saved.
It gives me time to learn **judgment**, which I need.
do: Pass my exams and ask for the **trickier online-seller** files.
Save **£200 a month** towards a house deposit with Paula.
Sketch a plan for my **own small practice**.
S0.quote: In my family, you don't really count as grown up until you've got your own name over a door.
fieldNote: He's ambitious, with a family history of **self-employment** shaping his goal.
He admits his **trust in the tools** causes rookie errors.
His only worry is **complacency**, which his partner has named.

steps.text: Pass the exams and take trickier online-seller files
Save £200 a month towards a house with Paula

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best time in years to start a small firm. At work I'd say we should be the ones using it, not the ones it's used against. Online I'd post about it more, probably to the point of being annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's an opening for me. If software does the first draft, one person can look after a hundred small businesses instead of thirty. Firms like ours will hire fewer juniors, but I don't plan to be a junior forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start taking on a few private clients on the side, gyms and cafés that my mates own, at a low fee. I'd pay for the best AI bookkeeping tools myself, about sixty pounds a month. And I'd put my savings towards a laptop and a professional insurance policy, so I can go solo in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like a door's opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it allowed, taking private clients while you're at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check my contract and talk to Mr Brennan first, because I'd want to do it straight. Some firms allow it if they're not competing clients. If not, I'd wait until I'm qualified and then leave properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The juniors who don't like the tools, I suppose. But I believe people can learn, and I'd rather see apprenticeships than handouts. If a gym owner can learn spreadsheets at forty, a junior accountant can learn the new tools at twenty-five.

say: I'd say it's the best time in years to **start a small firm**.
I'd say we should **use AI**, not have it used against us.
think: With software, one person can serve **a hundred** small businesses.
Firms hire fewer juniors, but I won't **stay junior** forever.
do: Take a few **private clients** on the side at a low fee.
Pay for the best **AI bookkeeping tools** myself, about £60 a month.
Put savings into a **laptop and insurance** to go solo in two years.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, like a door has opened.
S1.quote: If a gym owner can learn spreadsheets at forty, a junior accountant can learn the new tools at twenty-five.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as an **opening**, not a threat.
He insists on doing the side business **straight**, checking his contract first.
His **traditional views** show in preferring apprenticeships over handouts.

steps.text: Take on a few café and gym clients privately
Pay £60 a month for top AI bookkeeping tools
Buy a laptop and professional insurance to go solo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, though I'd say it more gently than that. It's going to be rough, but markets will find new work, they always have. I'd tell people to help their own families first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years is too fast even for me. AGI would do my job and my own small firm's job, so the business I planned is dead before it starts. Paula's physio is hands-on, so she's got until about 2031. My brother's removals firm is hands-on too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put part of my savings, maybe two thousand, into shares in the companies building this, so at least we own a bit of what replaces us. I'd go and work for my brother on removals while the firm still pays me, then full-time, because that's three years of robot-free work. And I'd ask Paula to marry me sooner, because I'd want us solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something. Scared of 2031, not 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why shares, when you're cutting everything else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if machines do the work, the people who own the machines get the money. I'd rather own a sliver than complain. I'm a free-market man, so I'd rather own a sliver of the robot than ask the government for a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your brother say about you lifting sofas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh for a week. Then he'd put me on the books and the bookings, and make me carry wardrobes on Saturdays. Family's family.

say: I'd say adapt, gently, because **markets find new work**.
I'd tell people to help their **own families** first.
think: Two years kills both my job and my **planned firm**.
Paula's physio and my brother's **removals** are hands-on till about 2031.
do: Put about **£2,000** into shares in AI companies.
Work for my **brother's removals** firm, then full-time.
S2.quote: I'm a free-market man, so I'd rather own a sliver of the robot than ask the government for a cheque.
fieldNote: Fast AGI ends his **business dream**, yet he keeps a sense of control.
He'd buy **shares** to own part of what replaces him, a free-market answer.
Family is his fallback: a **brother's removals** firm and an earlier wedding.

steps.text: Put about £2,000 into shares in AI companies
Join his brother's removals firm, doing books and lifting
Ask Paula to marry him sooner
Lean on his brother for steady work until robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, and people who move now will be fine. At work I'd tell the juniors to learn the tools and the clients. Online I'd share what I was doing, openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build my small firm and sell it before 2031. Small businesses will still want a person for a few years. If I time it right, I come out with something, not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify by 2028 and go solo straight after, with my café and gym clients. I'd run it almost entirely on AI tools, with maybe one part-time helper. And I'd aim to sell the client list to a bigger firm by 2030, before AGI makes it worthless, and put the money into a house with Paula.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a focused way. It's a race and I like races.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no one wants to buy the client list in 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have had three good years earning more than I would as an employee. I'd still have savings and a trade with my brother to fall back on. It's not all or nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd love it, he always said a man should own his work. My dad would also tell me to keep some cash under the mattress, and for once he'd be right.

say: I'd say five years is **a window** for people who move now.
I'd tell juniors to learn **the tools** and the clients.
think: I could build my firm and **sell it** before 2031.
Timed right, I come out with **something**, not nothing.
do: Run the firm on **AI tools** with one part-time helper.
Sell the **client list** by 2030 and buy a house with Paula.
S3.quote: My dad would also tell me to keep some cash under the mattress, and for once he'd be right.
fieldNote: He treats five years as a **business window**, planning to sell before it closes.
His fallback is **family**: savings and his brother's removals trade.
His father's advice on **ownership** and cash shapes the plan.

steps.text: Leave the firm to go solo after qualifying in 2028
Run the practice on AI tools with one helper
Sell the client list by 2030 and buy a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and there's no excuse not to use it. At work I'd say let's build something. Online I'd probably be the guy who keeps posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well in most of that decade. I'd have my own firm by thirty, a house, maybe kids, and I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes. I'd have time to move the business into something AI can't do, or sell it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go solo after qualifying, grow to maybe two hundred small clients with AI doing the processing, and hire one apprentice. I'd buy a house with Paula by 2029. And around 2033 I'd start moving the money into things that last, property, maybe a share in my brother's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, even. Ten years is plenty for someone who's ready to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprentice, if AI does the processing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone trained me, and I'd want to do the same. And clients still want a person to talk to for a while. I'd teach the apprentice the judgment side, the bit the tools don't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been confident throughout. Is there a version where it goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I get lazy. If I'm comfortable in 2034 and think I'm the exception. Comfort is the risk for a man like me, not the robots.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** with no excuse to waste.
At work I'd say **let's build** something.
think: I'd **do well** in most of that decade.
I'd have time to **sell well** or move the business before 2036.
do: Go solo and grow to about **200 small clients**.
Hire **one apprentice** to learn the judgment side.
S4.quote: Comfort is the risk for a man like me, not the robots.
fieldNote: A decade suits his **ambitions**, and he sees mostly upside.
He'd hire an **apprentice** out of gratitude, matching his traditional views.
He names **complacency** as his real risk, not AI.

steps.text: Grow a solo practice to 200 clients using AI tools
Buy a house with Paula by 2029
Buy into his brother's removals business around 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It kills the firm I've been planning since I was twenty-two, before I've even started it. What would help is fewer rules stopping small businesses from starting and hiring, and help for people like my brother to take on workers. Not handouts, ways to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people want to own. Everyone asks who loses their job to AI. Nobody asks who owns the AI, and that's what decides whether ordinary families come out ahead.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks who loses their job to AI. Nobody asks who owns the AI, and that's what decides whether ordinary families come out ahead.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old junior** serving cafés, gyms and online sellers, using AI tools daily.
He's quick but makes rookie errors, trusting **the tools** too much.
He dreams of his **own practice**, following a family line of self-employment.
Slower pictures look like **opportunity**; fast AGI sends him to his brother's removals firm.
Free-market views show in buying **shares** and wanting fewer rules, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which kills his planned firm before it starts.
whatWouldHelp: **Fewer rules** stopping small businesses starting and hiring.
Help for **family firms** to take on workers.
